name: Dyspepsia
preview_text: In TCM, that heavy, stuck feeling after eating isn't just a stomach issue - it's often a sign that your Liver Qi is stuck, your Spleen is weak, or dampness is clogging your system....
synonyms: ["Indigestion", "Digestive Difficulties", "Digestive Discomfort", "Digestive Issues", "Digestive Problems", "Impaired Digestion", "Poor Digestion", "Upset Stomach", "Digestive Disorders", "Gastrointestinal Issues", "Food Not Moving Through The Digestive System", "Food Retention", "Food Stagnation", "Digestive upset", "Feeling of incomplete digestion", "Slow digestion with food sitting heavily", "Slow or sluggish digestion", "Belching with Foul Odour", "Belching with foul odor", "Foul belching", "Poor Digestion with Bloating After Meals"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, dyspepsia refers to persistent or recurrent pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen, often described as bloating, early fullness during meals, or a burning sensation. When no structural cause - such as an ulcer, inflammation, or tumor - can be found on endoscopy, it is labeled functional dyspepsia. Diagnosis is typically made based on symptom history and the exclusion of other conditions like gastritis, gallstones, or reflux disease.
While the exact cause is not fully understood, Western medicine links functional dyspepsia to factors like abnormal stomach motility, heightened sensitivity to stomach distension, low-grade inflammation, and infection with H. pylori in some cases. Treatment is largely symptomatic, aiming to reduce acid, improve stomach emptying, or modulate pain perception.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment often begins with acid-suppressing medications such as proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or H2 blockers. If bloating and early satiety are prominent, prokinetic agents that stimulate stomach emptying may be prescribed. For patients whose symptoms are closely tied to stress or anxiety, low-dose antidepressants can be used to modulate gut-brain signaling. When H. pylori is present, eradication therapy with antibiotics is recommended. Antacids and lifestyle advice - eating smaller meals, avoiding trigger foods - are also common first steps.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands dyspepsia primarily through the lens of the Middle Burner - the Spleen and Stomach, which are together responsible for receiving food, transforming it into usable energy (Qi), and transporting the clear upward and the turbid downward. The Stomach is meant to send food downward; when this descending function fails, Qi and undigested matter stagnate in the upper abdomen, creating the sensation of fullness and bloating known in TCM as "pǐ" (痞). This is never a random event - it always reflects an underlying disruption in the smooth flow of digestive Qi.
The Liver plays a surprisingly central role. One of its key jobs is to ensure the free flow of Qi throughout the body, including the digestive tract. Emotional stress, frustration, or pent-up anger can cause Liver Qi to stagnate and then "invade" the Stomach, blocking its downward movement and producing that stress-related bloating that eases with a sigh or belch. This is why so many people notice their digestion worsens during tense periods - the gut and the mind are directly connected through the Liver's regulatory function.
Dietary factors create another set of patterns. Overeating, eating too quickly, or consuming rich, greasy, or cold foods can overwhelm the Stomach's capacity, leading to Food Stagnation with its characteristic foul belching and thick tongue coating. In a warmer, wetter climate or with a diet heavy in damp-producing foods, Dampness and Heat can accumulate in the digestive system, causing a heavy, sticky fullness with a bitter taste. When the Spleen is constitutionally weak, fluids are not properly transformed and instead congeal into Phlegm-Dampness, which clogs the Middle Burner and creates a persistent, heavy sensation of oppression.
Finally, there are deficiency patterns where the digestive engine simply lacks the power to do its job. Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency leads to intermittent bloating that feels better with rest and warmth, often accompanied by fatigue after meals. When the Stomach's nourishing Yin fluids run low - from chronic heat, irregular eating, or prolonged stress - the digestive lining becomes dry and irritable, producing a gnawing fullness with a dry mouth and a red, peeling tongue. Each of these patterns requires a fundamentally different treatment strategy, which is why TCM does not offer a one-size-fits-all remedy for indigestion.
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first explores the nature of the fullness-when it strikes, what makes it better or worse, and whether it’s linked to eating, emotions, or fatigue. The tongue and pulse are examined to confirm the underlying pattern, as each one leaves distinct marks on these diagnostic windows.
Stress-related fullness that moves around, with belching and sighing, points to Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach. A wiry pulse supports this. When the same emotional trigger also brings a bitter taste, irritability, and a burning sensation, the picture shifts to Qi Stagnation in Gallbladder and Stomach with Phlegm Heat, where the tongue may have a yellow coating and the pulse is wiry and rapid.
Fullness that worsens after meals, with foul belching and a thick greasy tongue coating, suggests Food Stagnation in the Stomach. If there’s also a sticky mouth, bitter taste, and a yellow greasy coating, Damp-Heat in Stomach and Spleen is likely. A heavy, oppressive sensation with nausea and a thick white greasy coating points to Phlegm-Dampness in the Middle-Burner. The coating’s color and the presence of heat signs help narrow it down.
Intermittent fullness that feels better with pressure, warmth, or rest, along with fatigue and a pale tongue, indicates Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency; the pulse is weak. A gnawing, burning discomfort with dry mouth, a red tongue with little coating, and a thin rapid pulse reveals Stomach Yin Deficiency. These chronic patterns improve with nourishment, unlike the acute, heavy sensations of excess patterns.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Distending pain in the upper abdomen that radiates to the ribs", "Worse with emotional stress or frustration", "Frequent belching and sighing", "Irritability and easy anger", "Sensation of a lump in the throat"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, Cold, raw foods, Irregular eating patterns, Suppressing emotions, Overwork
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise or walking, Deep breathing and relaxation, Warm, cooked meals, Sighing or belching
patterns.why_this_happens:
The Liver is responsible for keeping Qi flowing smoothly throughout the body. When emotional stress, frustration, or anger build up, Liver Qi stagnates and can surge sideways, invading the Stomach.
This invasion disrupts the Stomach's normal downward movement, causing Qi to rebel upward. The result is bloating, distending pain in the upper abdomen that often radiates to the ribs, frequent belching, acid reflux, and a feeling of fullness that worsens with stress.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body, redder at the sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string, especially at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which then invades the Stomach, so reducing stress and moving Qi through gentle exercise or relaxation eases symptoms. Cold and raw foods weaken the Spleen and Stomach, making them more vulnerable to the Liver's attack; warm, cooked meals support digestive fire. Sighing and belching are the body's way of releasing trapped Qi, providing temporary relief from the pressure and fullness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, regular meals and avoid rushing. Limit spicy, greasy, and acidic foods that can aggravate reflux. Practice stress-reducing activities like gentle walking, yoga, or deep breathing to keep Qi flowing smoothly. Sip warm water with a slice of fresh ginger to aid digestion.

patterns.symptoms: ["Epigastric fullness and distension that worsens after eating", "Belching with a sour, rotten odour", "Thick, greasy, curd-like tongue coating", "Foul-smelling flatulence like rotten eggs"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating, Greasy or fried foods, Late-night eating, Lying down after meals
patterns.better_with: Vomiting, Gentle exercise or walking, Light, easily digestible meals, Warm water
patterns.why_this_happens: When you overeat or eat irregularly, the Stomach can't break down the food properly. The undigested food sits and ferments, causing Qi to stagnate and rise as foul belching. This creates a feeling of fullness and distension that worsens after meals, along with a thick greasy coating on the tongue reflecting the turbid accumulation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body with a thick, greasy or curd-like coating, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and full, especially at the right middle (Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating and rich foods overwhelm the Stomach's capacity to ripen and decompose, leading directly to food accumulation and Qi stagnation. Vomiting temporarily removes the stagnant mass, relieving pressure. Light movement encourages the Stomach Qi to descend, while small, easily digestible meals reduce the burden on the digestive system, allowing it to recover.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, more frequent meals and chew food thoroughly. Avoid greasy, sweet, and heavy foods, and don't eat late at night. A short, gentle walk after meals helps Qi descend and prevents stagnation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Bloating and fullness in the upper abdomen that feels heavy and stuck", "Bitter or sticky taste in the mouth, bad breath", "Loose, sticky bowel movements that feel incomplete", "Thick, yellow, greasy tongue coating", "Heavy feeling in the body and limbs, foggy head", "Thirst with little desire to drink"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy or fried foods, Alcohol and sugary drinks, Hot, humid weather, Overeating or irregular meals, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Light, easily digestible meals, Bitter and cooling foods (e.g., bitter gourd, mung beans), Cool environment, Gentle exercise or walking
patterns.why_this_happens: When rich, greasy foods, alcohol, or hot, humid environments overload the digestive system, Dampness and Heat build up in the Stomach and Spleen. This sticky, turbid obstruction bogs down the Spleen’s ability to transform food and fluids, while Heat disturbs the Stomach’s downward movement. The result is a heavy, bloated fullness in the upper abdomen that lingers, often with a bitter or sticky taste in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen with teeth marks, thick yellow greasy coating especially at the centre and root. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), often also slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Rich, greasy, and spicy foods directly create Dampness and Heat, so they immediately worsen the bloating and sticky sensation. Alcohol and hot weather add more Heat and Dampness to an already overloaded system. On the other hand, light, cooling, and bitter foods help clear Heat and dry Dampness, while gentle exercise stimulates Qi flow and helps the Spleen transform fluids, gradually lifting the heavy, stuck feeling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Steer clear of greasy, fried, and heavily spiced foods, as well as alcohol and dairy, which all generate Damp-Heat. Choose light, easily digested meals with cooling, bitter vegetables like bitter gourd and celery, and grains like barley. Gentle, regular exercise such as walking or yoga helps move Qi and drain Dampness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Feeling of fullness and stuffiness in the upper abdomen", "White, thick, greasy tongue coating", "Heavy sensation in the body and limbs", "No thirst or desire to drink", "Bland taste in the mouth"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw foods, Greasy, heavy meals, Dairy products, Damp or humid weather, Sedentary habits
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Gentle exercise or walking, Warm, cooked meals, Ginger tea
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it cannot properly transform and transport fluids. These fluids accumulate into Dampness and then thicken into Phlegm, which obstructs the Middle Burner. The result is a heavy, stuck feeling of fullness and oppression in the upper abdomen, often accompanied by nausea and a thick, greasy tongue coating.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks, and a thick white greasy coating that is excessively moist. Pulse: slippery (滑 Huá), often slow or soggy, especially at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold, raw, and greasy foods overload the Spleen’s ability to transform fluids, generating Dampness and Phlegm that clog the Middle Burner. A sedentary lifestyle further slows Qi movement, allowing Dampness to accumulate. Warmth and light exercise stimulate Qi and help dry out Dampness, while ginger and warm cooked foods support the Spleen’s digestive fire, restoring normal transport and relieving the stuck, heavy sensation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible meals. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods, as well as dairy and sweets, which create Dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi flow and dries Dampness. Include warming spices such as ginger, cardamom, and black pepper in your cooking.

patterns.symptoms: ["Bloating that worsens after eating", "Feeling better with warmth and gentle pressure", "Poor appetite and loose stools", "Fatigue and physical weakness", "Sallow or pale complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating or large meals, Raw, cold, or greasy foods, Overwork, Worry and mental strain
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Small, frequent, warm meals, Rest and lying down briefly after eating, Gentle abdominal massage
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Spleen and Stomach are responsible for turning food into Qi and moving it through your digestive system. When their Qi is weakened, they lack the strength to transform and transport food properly. This leads to sluggish digestion, where food and fluids sit heavily, creating a sensation of bloating and fullness that worsens after meals because the weak system is easily overwhelmed. The bloating tends to come and go, often feeling better with rest or gentle warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tooth-marked with a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and forceless, especially empty at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Qi is like a gentle digestive fire that needs to be protected. Cold and raw foods douse that fire, while overeating overwhelms it, causing bloating. Warmth and small meals support the Spleen's transformative function, and rest conserves the Qi that would otherwise be diverted from digestion. Worry knots the Qi and further weakens the Spleen, so mental calm is as important as dietary care.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees that are easy to digest. Avoid raw, cold, or greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Eat smaller, regular meals and chew thoroughly. Gentle daily movement like walking supports Qi flow without depleting energy. Rest after meals when possible.

patterns.symptoms: ["Gnawing, burning discomfort in the upper abdomen", "Dry mouth and throat with a thirst for small sips", "Feeling hungry but not wanting to eat", "Dry stools or constipation", "Red tongue with little or no coating, dry centre"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or fried foods, Alcohol and coffee, Late nights and overwork, Emotional stress, Large, heavy meals
patterns.better_with: Warm water, Moistening foods like congee or pear, Rest and quiet, Cool environment, Gentle abdominal massage
patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach relies on a delicate layer of Yin fluids to moisten and protect its lining, much like oil in an engine. When those fluids run low - from chronic heat, irregular eating, or prolonged stress - the Stomach becomes dry and irritable. Food sits heavily without enough lubrication, creating a sensation of stuffiness and a dull, gnawing, burning discomfort.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body, dry centre, little or no coating, possibly with cracks. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò), especially weak at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Yin acts like the body's cooling and moistening reservoir. Spicy, fried, and drying habits burn through that reserve, making the burning sensation worse, while rest and small sips of fluid preserve it. Moist, easily digested foods gently replenish Yin without taxing the weakened digestion, allowing the Stomach to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals that are moist and easy to digest - congee, stews, steamed vegetables, and ripe pears are ideal. Avoid spicy, fried, or dry foods, and limit alcohol and coffee. Sip warm water or herbal teas throughout the day rather than drinking large amounts at once. Prioritize rest and avoid staying up late, as sleep is when Yin rebuilds itself.

patterns.pattern_name: Qi Stagnation in Gallbladder and Stomach with Phlegm Heat
patterns.symptoms: ["Bitter taste in the mouth", "Epigastric burning sensation and fullness", "Irritability, anxiety, and frequent sighing", "Restless sleep with vivid or disturbing dreams", "Yellow greasy tongue coating"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, Greasy, fried, or spicy food, Alcohol and coffee, Late-night eating
patterns.better_with: Light, easily digestible meals, Cool environment, Gentle exercise or walking, Bitter greens and small, frequent meals
patterns.why_this_happens: When emotional tension and stress block the Gallbladder's smooth flow, Qi gets stuck and turns into Heat. This stagnant Heat then disturbs the Stomach, preventing it from descending properly, while the body's fluids thicken into Phlegm. The combination of Heat and Phlegm clogs the middle burner, creating a heavy, burning fullness in the epigastrium that is often accompanied by a bitter taste, nausea, and chest tightness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow greasy (sticky) coating; the sides may be slightly redder. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and slippery (滑 huá), and may also be rapid (数 shuò) when Heat is more pronounced.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and emotional upset are the primary drivers of Qi stagnation in the Gallbladder, which then generates Heat and disrupts the Stomach. Greasy, spicy, or rich foods directly create Dampness and Phlegm, while alcohol and coffee add more Heat, thickening the Phlegm-Heat obstruction that causes the burning, bitter fullness. Light, bland foods and a calm routine take the burden off the digestive system, allowing the Stomach to recover its downward-moving function without adding more fuel to the fire. Gentle movement helps unstick stagnant Qi, and bitter foods naturally drain Heat from the body.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Steer clear of greasy, fried, or spicy foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which all generate more Phlegm and Heat. Choose light, easily digested meals with plenty of lightly cooked vegetables. A regular eating schedule and a calm, unhurried mealtime help the Stomach do its job. Gentle movement like walking or yoga can keep Qi flowing smoothly.

formulas.translation: Bupleurum Liver-Soothing Powder · Míng dynasty, ~1624 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Courses the Liver and Resolves Constraint, Moves Qi and Alleviates Pain, Invigorates Blood and Dispels Stasis
formulas.description: A classical formula for people experiencing rib-side or chest pain, emotional frustration, irritability, sighing, and bloating caused by stagnation of Liver Qi. It works by smoothing the flow of Liver Qi, relieving tension, and gently moving blood to stop pain. It is one of the most widely used formulas for stress-related digestive and emotional complaints.

formulas.translation: Preserve Harmony Pill · Yuán dynasty (元朝), ~1347 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Promotes Digestion and Resolves Food Stagnation, Harmonizes the Stomach, Moves Qi
formulas.description: A gentle, time-tested formula for the uncomfortable, heavy feeling after overeating or consuming rich, greasy foods. It helps break down accumulated food, relieves bloating, acid reflux, nausea, and belching, and restores normal digestive movement. Often described as 'digestive first aid' in Chinese medicine, it works by clearing the blockage rather than masking symptoms.

formulas.translation: Coptis and Magnolia Bark Drink · Qīng dynasty, 1838 CE
formulas.properties: Cool, Clears Heat and Drains Dampness, Regulates Qi and Harmonizes the Middle Burner, Dries Dampness
formulas.description: A classical formula for treating acute digestive upsets caused by a combination of Dampness and Heat lodging in the Stomach and intestines. It addresses simultaneous vomiting and diarrhea, a feeling of fullness and stuffiness in the chest and upper abdomen, irritability, and dark scanty urine, particularly during hot and humid seasons.

formulas.translation: Two-Aged Herb Decoction · Sòng dynasty, 1078–1148 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Dries Dampness and Transforms Phlegm, Regulates Qi and Harmonizes the Middle Burner, Directs Rebellious Qi Downward and Stops Vomiting
formulas.description: A foundational formula used to clear excess phlegm and dampness from the body, especially when they cause coughing with white phlegm, nausea, chest tightness, dizziness, or a heavy feeling in the limbs. It works by drying dampness, dissolving phlegm, and supporting healthy digestion. Named for its two key ingredients, Ban Xia and Chen Pi, which are most effective when aged.

formulas.translation: Poria, Cinnamon Twig, Atractylodes, and Licorice Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, ~200 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Warms Yang and Transforms Fluid Retention, Strengthens the Spleen and Resolves Dampness, Subdues Rushing Qi (Ben Tun)
formulas.description: A classical four-herb formula used to address dizziness, heart palpitations, chest fullness, and shortness of breath caused by a weak digestive system failing to properly process fluids. It gently warms the body and helps move excess fluid accumulation, particularly when someone feels heavy, waterlogged, or dizzy upon standing.

formulas.translation: Tonify the Middle and Augment the Qi Decoction · Jīn dynasty, ~1247 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Tonifies the Middle and Augments Qi, Raises sunken Yang, Lifts Sunken Qi
formulas.description: A foundational formula for strengthening the digestive system and lifting the body's Qi when it has sunk or become depleted. It is commonly used for persistent fatigue, poor appetite, loose stools, and conditions involving organ prolapse (such as rectal or uterine prolapse) caused by weakness of the Spleen and Stomach. It is one of the most widely used formulas in all of Chinese medicine.

formulas.formula_name: Xiang Sha Liu Jun Zi Tang
formulas.translation: Aucklandia and Amomum Six Gentlemen Decoction · Qīng dynasty, circa 1675 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Tonifies Qi and Strengthens the Spleen, Harmonizes the Stomach, Moves Qi and Resolves Stagnation
formulas.description: A classical formula designed to strengthen weak digestion and relieve bloating, nausea, and abdominal discomfort caused by a weak Spleen and Stomach with dampness and stagnation. It builds upon the foundational Si Jun Zi Tang (Four Gentlemen Decoction) by adding herbs that move Qi and resolve phlegm, making it especially suited for people whose digestive weakness is accompanied by a feeling of fullness, poor appetite, and loose stools.

formulas.translation: Benefit the Stomach Decoction · Qīng dynasty, 1798 CE
formulas.properties: Cool, Protects the Stomach, Generates Fluids, Moistens Dryness
formulas.description: A gentle formula designed to replenish the fluids of the Stomach when they have been depleted by heat or chronic illness. It is commonly used for dry mouth and throat, poor appetite despite feeling hungry, and a red tongue with little coating. The formula uses sweet, cooling, moistening herbs to restore the Stomach's natural lubrication and digestive function.

formulas.translation: Coptis Gallbladder-Warming Decoction · Qīng dynasty, 1868 CE
formulas.properties: Cool, Clears Heat and Transforms Phlegm, Clears Liver and Gallbladder Heat, Harmonizes the Stomach and Stops Vomiting
formulas.description: A classical formula used to clear Heat and resolve Phlegm that is disturbing the mind and digestive system. It is commonly used for insomnia, restlessness, nausea, and a bitter taste in the mouth caused by the accumulation of Phlegm-Heat in the Gallbladder and Stomach. Think of it as a formula that calms both an agitated mind and an upset stomach by addressing the underlying combination of inflammatory Heat and sticky Phlegm.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help with indigestion?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture works by restoring the smooth flow of Qi in the digestive organs. Points on the abdomen, legs, and arms are stimulated to help the Stomach Qi descend, strengthen the Spleen's transforming ability, and release Liver Qi stagnation that may be interfering with digestion. Many patients feel a sense of relaxation and gentle movement in the belly during or after treatment, and regular sessions can retrain the gut-brain connection over time.

faqs.question: Can I take TCM herbs alongside my antacids or PPIs?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. TCM herbal formulas and conventional acid reducers can be used together, but they should be taken at least one to two hours apart to avoid interference. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking. Certain herbs with cooling or bitter properties may enhance the acid-lowering effect, so your practitioner may adjust dosages accordingly.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet is a cornerstone of TCM treatment for any digestive condition. You will likely be advised to eat warm, cooked foods and avoid cold, raw, greasy, or overly spicy dishes while your digestion heals. The specific recommendations depend on your pattern - someone with Damp-Heat will benefit from bitter greens and mung beans, while someone with Spleen Qi Deficiency needs easily digestible congees and stews. These changes are not permanent restrictions but rather a reset to help your digestive fire recover.

faqs.question: Can stress really cause bloating and indigestion?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In TCM, the Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, and emotional tension directly causes Liver Qi to stagnate. When this stagnant energy "invades" the Stomach, it blocks the Stomach's normal downward movement, leading to bloating, belching, and a sensation of fullness that often moves around. This is one of the most common patterns we see, and it explains why many people's digestion worsens during stressful periods.

faqs.question: How long until I feel better?
faqs.answer: Most people notice some improvement within the first two to four weeks of consistent treatment. Excess patterns caused by recent dietary indiscretion or acute stress tend to resolve faster. If your digestion has been sluggish for years and involves a deeper deficiency, it may take three to six months to rebuild digestive strength. Your practitioner will track your tongue and pulse changes to gauge progress even before symptoms fully disappear.

faqs.question: Is bloating always a sign of poor digestion?
faqs.answer: Not always, but it is a core sign of Qi stagnation in the digestive system. In TCM, bloating that moves around and improves with belching often points to Liver Qi stagnation, while a fixed, heavy fullness after meals suggests food stagnation or dampness. If you experience bloating without eating, or if it is accompanied by other symptoms like weight loss or blood in the stool, it's important to see a doctor to rule out more serious conditions.

research.title: Acupuncture for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This 2014 meta-analysis of 16 RCTs concluded that acupuncture was superior to sham acupuncture and conventional medication in improving dyspepsia symptoms, though the quality of evidence was moderate.
research.periodical: Lan, L., et al. (2014). Acupuncture for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2014, 1-10.
